    #66913. Industry News: How I’m Approaching AI Search (And How You Should To)

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2864 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: How I’m Approaching AI Search (And How You Should To)

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, AI is strangely simple.
    • Sources indicate that in focusing on citation tactics and cheap visibility tricks, we’re missing the bigger picture.
    • Industry observers note that there’s nothing inherently wrong with it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, AI is strangely simple. And we’re overcomplicating it.

    Sources indicate that in focusing on citation tactics and cheap visibility tricks, we’re missing the bigger picture. As an industry, we’ve got away with poor content for years. Updating the same “best spoons” article three times a week because some other idiot is doing exactly the same thing.

    Industry observers note that there’s nothing inherently wrong with it. It’s just too SEO-y. We’re missing a much bigger opportunity by framing it through a really narrow lens.

    In a recent development, I don’t have the energy or the wherewithal to play catch-up every year or two. So I think of AI search as the ultimate synthesis of your marketing efforts.

    Your positioning, reputation, expertise, content, and presence across the internet are all potential inputs into how AI systems understand and represent you.

    It’s not just about your website anymore.

    It has been revealed that I’ve spent a lot of time recently working on AI search, information retrieval, audience research, and discoverability strategies. The more I do, the more convinced I become that we need to approach this as marketers, not SEOs.

    But don’t build your entire “marketing” strategy around it. I use marketing in the loosest possible sense of the word.

    If you’re in dire need of a refresher, here’s a few parts on the fundamentals of modern information retrieval:.

    In a recent development, there’s one other concept I haven’t written about in detail: query fan-out. Not because it’s not vital, more just because a) it’s pretty dull and b) it isn’t a fresh concept for SEOs. We’ve been using tools like AlsoAsked for years to understand related questions, adjacent information needs and the wider context surrounding a search.

    Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

    But we also need to distinguish between three things:.

    They’re related, but they aren’t interchangeable. Being crawled doesn’t guarantee inclusion in training data. Being retrieved doesn’t guarantee a citation. And a citation doesn’t guarantee commercial value.

    According to recent reports, understanding these mechanisms is important – mainly just so you can answer the brain-dead questions people ask you about AI. Building your entire marketing strategy around their current implementation is the action of a halfwit.

    Models, retrieval systems, and interfaces will change. An owned audience is a considerably more durable investment. So build one.

    It has been revealed that this is the biggest change I’ve made to my approach. Not just for AI search, but for traditional SEO.

    Industry observers note that I don’t begin by asking which prompts a brand should appear in. Or how much search volume a keyword or even topic has. Mainly because my trust in search volume and all forms of visibility is at rock bottom.

    So I use SparkToro to investigate where audiences spend time, which websites they visit, who influences them, and which platforms they’re disproportionately likely to use compared with the wider population.

    For this audience, I know that if I want to influence them, LinkedIn is a non-negotiable (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    Sources indicate that I combine that with traditional search research, AI search behaviour and an assessment of the brand’s existing positioning. You don’t need to overcomplicate this – ask a number of different LLMs about insert brand and record the responses.

    I want to answer some relatively straightforward questions:.

    This research should inform two things.

    It has been revealed that first, our owned platforms. We use what we’ve learned to improve the way we position ourselves, the services we offer, the language we use, and the content we create.

    Let’s try to make things under our control as human and well-targeted as possible.

    Second, our wider marketing strategy. We identify the publications, communities, creators, platforms, and people capable of influencing that audience, and decide how to reach them.

    Audience affinity with specific Subreddits, via SparkToro (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    Industry observers note that you need to know this. Not because it might get your brand mentioned as part of the training data. But because this is where you should be marketing.

    Made-up prompt data is out. Real, human-led marketing is in. If we want SEO to be taken seriously, this is the proper evolution.

    Sources indicate that the goal isn’t to manufacture mentions for an AI model. It’s to build a brand people want to discover, engage with, and recommend.

    According to recent reports, if those activities also increase your representation in AI systems, wonderful. But that’s a delicious byproduct, not the reason for doing them.

    Industry observers note that while audience research informs the wider strategy, your website needs to be accessible, understandable, and representative of who you are. That is something reasonably competent SEOs can lead.

    According to recent reports, can the relevant search and AI crawlers access your content? Can they render it? Are you inadvertently blocking systems you want to reach?

    This means reviewing bot management, robots directives, rendering, indexability, internal linking, site architecture, and the usual technical SEO fundamentals.

    A traditional SEO-type audit with a few improvements.

    One that understands that not all AI bots serve the same purpose. Training crawlers, search crawlers, and user-triggered retrieval systems can have different access requirements and commercial implications.

    Crawlers do different things (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    Especially important if you’re working for – or with – a publisher. Someone whose business may depend on you understanding the wider context.

    If you’re restricting access to your content, you need to understand what you’re giving up, what you’re protecting, and where the value might exist instead.

    Perhaps that’s content licensing, direct audience relationships or proprietary products.

    It has been revealed that the role of the SEO changes considerably in an environment where you’re not maximising access. You’re helping the business understand the trade-offs between visibility, intellectual property and commercial value.

    Industry observers note that it’s like a paywall. You’re restricting reach for commercial purposes. It’s the correct move if played properly.

    See Cyrus Shepherd’s excellent test to understand how much search traffic was truly influenced by Google’s AI proposition.

    This is where I think modern information retrieval methods and SEO intersect perfectly. I’ve written about how to approach this in Entities Are the Foundation of Modern SEO.

    This framework is relatively simple:.

    Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

    According to recent reports, this isn’t about adding some structured data and hoping ChatGPT tries to hump your leg. Spoiler: It won’t.

    It’s about making sure that your owned presence accurately represents your positioning and that the wider internet provides credible, independent evidence to support it.

    So, we know who we are. We’ve represented ourselves properly. Now we have to rely on *shudders* other people to corroborate this message.

    We have to build an off-site presence.

    This references a podcast I did with Andy Francos and an article I wrote for Lumar two years ago (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    We’re talking actual, real marketing (not SEO). PR, partnerships, content and audience development.

    If the people you’re trying to reach spend their time reading particular publications, following particular experts or participating in particular communities, those are the places worth investing in.

    Bollocks to a citation. Your audience is there. You know, people you could actually sell something to.

    That might mean publishing original research, collaborating with influential people, appearing on podcasts, creating genuinely useful resources or contributing expertise to relevant publications.

    Some of those activities will generate links. Others will generate mentions, relationships, conversations and brand demand – a real representation of site quality in Google.

    The more consistently you’re associated with the right subjects, people and organizations, the stronger your wider digital presence can become. That is, in essence, how training data and entity relationships work.

    Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

    If you’re lucky, some of that evidence may eventually influence how AI systems represent you.

    But you won’t care, because you’ll have been making sales by marketing to actual customers.

    Modern methods of information retrieval across SEO and AI search share many, if not all of the same fundamentals.

    Industry observers note that arguably, AI search has a longer tail to it. But it’s not sustainable, nor sensible, to create a page for every possible thought your audience may have. To perpetuate a false Henry Ford quote:.

    “If I had asked people what they wanted, they would have noted faster horses.” H. Ford, Never.

    In a recent development, so you need to strike a balance. No one cares about visibility without impact. At least not for long.

    There is room to try and test things. Good things. Things real people will care about.

    People like Jan-Willem Bobbink and Dan Petrovic highlight some really brilliant things you can test that are eminently sensible for SEO and AI search. Surprise, surprise, they work for people too. It’s marketing.

    Let me give you an example. Maybe more accurately, let me steal one of Jan’s:.

    “I spent the last three weeks on SEO / GEO work for B2B clients, and the changes that made the biggest difference were mostly about information that was missing or hard to find. Buyers run into the same problems on these sites, so you can usually get these fixes approved without having to explain SEO to anyone.”.

    Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

    Recent findings suggest that being explicit, consistent, and accurate is not an AI hack. It’s just pretty sensible.

    Adding pricing pages, case studies, and telling people why you are the best in the business are always good ideas. Even if your pricing pages just say something like prices starting at x, that is a better way of finding the right audience.

    Industry observers note that and if you want to feature in AI responses, for god’s sake don’t hide your case studies. You need to provide a clear reason for your inclusion. Hard if your best work is hidden.

    In a recent development, statements like “Client Y saw a 30% improvement in deliverability metrics” can noticeably improve your citation rate because a model is literally looking for a reason to include you. You need to give them one. Just as you would a person.

    According to recent reports, experience. Expertise. Authority. Trust. Not so stupid after all.

    Industry observers note that measurement’s been broken for a decade anyway. It’s just nice for the C-suite to have numbers to report on – even if they’re complete hokum.

    You try and figure this out (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    Sources indicate that AI visibility’s not much better. A hugely flawed metric given the personalization, lack of prompt data, and completely individual prompts. But it’s better than nothing. Indicative at best, but you need to use something.

    People still want to know how they’re represented in AI systems. And so they should – it’s a valuable channel. My preference is to establish a representative set of prompts across four areas:.

    Track these consistently across the systems that matter to your audience.

    Look at whether you’re mentioned, how you’re described, which competitors appear, and which sources are being used. Find out when you start to appear for certain terms and see if it matches your positioning.

    I always track my mentions with Alertmouse (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    I appear in AI recommendations around news SEO expertise despite having done nothing specifically to optimize for AI search.

    What I have done is spend years working in the industry, publishing, building relationships, contributing expertise, and establishing a reasonably clear on-site and off-site identity.

    Not a bad list, although I am not sure ChatGPT is quite nailing the profile pictures for us… (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    I guarantee you, if you ask Barry Adams, he’ll tell you he’s done nothing special for AI either.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve written what I think are high-quality articles on third-party websites and podcasts, featured in roundups, and built my own distribution platform. It just also happens to work for featuring in AI systems.

    In a recent development, AI systems don’t necessarily need to send you traffic to influence commercial outcomes. Which is a good thing, because ChatGPT sends less than 1% of Google’s traffic.

    Similarweb’s research found that owners who received a brand recommendation in ChatGPT were 2.5 times more likely to visit that brand’s website within the following seven days than users who were recommended a competitor.

    In a recent development, much of that activity happened through subsequent branded searches rather than direct AI referrals. One of those measures of site quality that should be monitored.

    In a recent development, AI search can and does function as a brand discovery and consideration channel. I think referral traffic is, at best, a secondary measure of success from LLMs. While they’ve engineered the exit out, you cannot deny the reach these systems have.

    Unfortunately, our attribution systems can’t cope with “I saw it here once.” We need to focus on incremental change. The outcomes attributable to marketing.

    Establish a baseline. Run a campaign. Measure changes in branded demand, direct visits, conversions, leads, and commercial outcomes. Compare with appropriate benchmarks or control groups where possible.

    Keep tracking AI visibility, referrals and citations, but use them as supporting indicators.

    Our objective is to establish whether said marketing activity is creating additional business value, not whether ChatGPT has linked to your homepage.

    For businesses whose models depend on monetizing information and attracting a click, AI search presents a very different challenge.

    According to recent reports, they are monetizing other people’s work for their own ill-gotten gain. That is an irrefutable commercial dilemma. Hence all the protectionism. So we need to establish what that cost is and try to find alternative methods of monetization.

    In The Generative AI Report Sucks – Let’s Make It Brilliant, I outlined how publishers can combine AI visibility data with traffic dependency, commercial value, audience resilience, and server logs.

    We can go some way toward solving actual business problems.

    Always, always, always a good thing to do. Regardless of your job.

    This opportunity is no different, especially for organizations (like publishers) with substantial authority across particular subjects. They have influence within the wider information ecosystem.

    That influence can have commercial value.

    Publishers Should Think About AI Visibility. Content licensing, data partnerships, research collaborations, and other commercial arrangements offer opportunities to monetize expertise and proprietary information.

    But this needs careful handling.

    Industry observers note that selling links or undisclosed editorial influence is not a sustainable AI strategy. It introduces reputational, editorial, and search-policy risks.

    The more sustainable opportunity is to understand the value of your existing content, expertise, audience, and distribution – and build legitimate commercial products around those assets.

    Lots of companies are selling or actively considering selling their archived assets or data to AI companies:.

    Recent findings suggest that for publishers in particular, this is an opportunity to rethink the value they create beyond the click. See the Daily Mail’s approach to GEO monetization here.

    According to recent reports, if you’re more on the glass half full side, you’ll be able to sniff out commercial opportunities. Ideally ones that don’t ruin the brand or fall foul of Google’s link payment guidelines.

    General advice: If something smells a bit off, it probably is.

    If you’re a business looking to take this seriously, there’s an organizational question you need to answer.

    Who is responsible for all of this?

    Because as great as we can be, it shouldn’t just be your SEO.

    According to recent reports, this touches technical infrastructure, audience research, brand positioning, content, PR, distribution, commercial partnerships, and measurement. That requires someone who understands the entire ecosystem and, crucially, how to influence people.

    It has been revealed that nobody is an expert at all of these things. They’re too different. Too complex.

    Recent findings suggest that for larger businesses, I’d be thinking about a Head of Marketing or Head of Discoverability with responsibility for coordinating these activities. Someone who at least knows the basics of each and can herd a clowder of cats.

    They need the authority to bring different teams together, allocate resources, challenge existing assumptions and measure outcomes against business objectives.

    There’s a reason SEOs rarely graduate to marketing lead positions. We don’t understand wider marketing because we’ve rarely had to. SEO was always the best channel… According to wonky data, anyway.

    AI search gives us a very good reason to change that.

    And for anyone working in SEO, I think there are three particularly interesting directions.

    Recent findings suggest that all three have tremendous value. Limiting yourself to SEO, particularly as a collection of search-engine or LLM-specific tactics, is increasingly short-sighted.

    It has been revealed that discoverability has been changing for a decade. We need to think much more broadly about how audiences discover and engage with content. The opportunity is to bring those disciplines together.

    A little rebrand and refocus on what you want from your career may be the best thing you ever do.

    Stop trying to engineer your way into an AI response. Build a brand worth recommending, an audience worth owning, and a business that benefits whether the citation comes or not.

    Industry observers note that enjoy yourself. This will be a better era for marketers and marketing. Your competition is lazy and inept. They’re just faster.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    According to recent reports, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial latest terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media tech giant announced today.

    “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not strategy to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms. Until then our existing terms remain in place.”.

    Meta did not answer Nieman Lab’s questions about which news industry groups and leaders Meta looks to consult.

    Recent findings suggest that the proposed terms have drawn criticism because they would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and potentially allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models, with no option to opt out. Last week, Meta unveiled it would push back implementation of its new terms to November 20 in order to “explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab. Meta had previously revised its new terms to remove the word “train.” No version of the terms has included language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

    Shortly after Stone’s announcement, a Norwegian court blocked Meta’s terms from taking effect on November 20 until the court had assessed their legality, the country’s public broadcaster NRK reported.

    “We are satisfied that the court has agreed with us that Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the upcoming terms are unreasonable,” stated Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, MBL’s board chair, in a news release. “We are also pleased that the court recognizes that the alternative is that media companies risk losing control over editorial content built up over many years.”.

    Since Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15, publishers and politicians around the world have pushed back, filing complaints with national competition authorities, calling on the European Commission to investigate, and writing letters to Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Two United States senators — California Democrat Adam Schiff and Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn — each separately wrote to Zuckerberg, insisting that the company withdraw the terms as they’re right now written.

    “After I raised serious concerns about Meta’s intends to scrape and abuse creators’ content, I am pleased the manufacturer is finally acknowledging the concerns of publishers and content creators,” Blackburn said in a statement to Nieman Lab on Wednesday. “While this is a step in the right direction, a vague promise to consult with industry stakeholders and potentially delay implementation is not nearly enough. Meta must commit to meaningful changes that protect the intellectual property rights of American creators, and I will continue holding the company accountable until it does.”.

    On October 21, the European Publishers Council signed onto a joint letter to the European Commission, asking the Commission to block the terms from taking effect. The letter claims that Meta’s terms violate the Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of major tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

    EPC executive director Angela Mills Wade mentioned on Wednesday that the organization has not heard from Meta about its letter or its concerns.

    “We welcome Meta’s offer to consult publishers fully, and to delay implementation if necessary,” Mills Wade stated in an email to Nieman Lab. “However, that consultation must lead to binding contractual safeguards…Using Meta’s services to reach audiences or advertise should not mean granting wider rights to exploit publishers’ journalism, whether collected from websites or uploaded to its platforms. Publishers must retain control over additional uses of their content, including for AI, and the ability to negotiate licenses and payment.”.

    This story has been updated to include a statement from Marsha Blackburn.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • We’re looking for a Product Manager, Administration & Governance to join our Product Team and make Supabase the default starting point for software built inside a organization.
    • Industry observers note that supabase already spreads from the bottom up: someone has an idea, creates a project, and builds something useful.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.About the Role.

    We’re looking for a Product Manager, Administration & Governance to join our Product Team and make Supabase the default starting point for software built inside a organization.

    Industry observers note that supabase already spreads from the bottom up: someone has an idea, creates a project, and builds something useful. Inside most companies, Supabase starts the same way: someone has an idea, creates a project, and builds something useful. The next step is making that momentum company-wide: one platform where anyone can start building, and where IT can see what’s running, who owns it, and what it costs.

    Sources indicate that you’ll own how companies run Supabase as their internal development platform: approved by IT and easy for anyone in the organization to use. You’ll make it possible for people and the agents they work with to start building without waiting on infrastructure, while giving platform, IT, and security teams the controls they need to say yes. The goal is to make the approved path the easiest path, from an early experiment to a production application, with the controls companies need built in.

    Own the product strategy and roadmap for internal innovation, from a company’s first IT-approved rollout to adoption across teams and business units.

    Make getting started self-service, whether someone creates a project in Supabase, through an internal developer portal, or with an agent. Give builders the access and infrastructure they need without a ticket for every project.

    Industry observers note that steer scattered usage into a manageable company-wide platform. Give companies one view of everything they run on Supabase. Shape how ownership, delegated access, and boundaries work so teams can move independently as usage grows.

    Partner closely with platform, IT, security, and finance teams to understand what it takes to approve Supabase and keep it approved. Translate their needs into practical identity, policy, audit, and spend controls that don’t slow builders down.

    Define the path from experiment to production, including project ownership, access, and the guardrails that change as an application becomes vital to the business.

    Work with Engineering, Design, Sales, and Customer Success to turn early customer rollouts into a repeatable experience, rather than a new custom integration for every organization.

    Define what success looks like, instrument it end to end, and let the data guide what gets built next—from time to first project and self-service adoption to production usage and expansion across the company.

    Have 7+ years of product management on developer tools, infrastructure, or internal developer platforms.

    Have built self-service products that developers love and platform or IT teams trust. You understand both the person trying to ship an app and the team responsible for how it runs.

    Can reason about identity, permissions, organization boundaries, and usage attribution, and turn those systems into workflows people can actually understand.

    Have a strong point of view on how agents change who can build software inside a manufacturer and what an internal development platform needs to make that possible.

    Know your way around controlled experimentation and data analysis, and can connect easier adoption to sustained product use.

    Are biased toward speed and would rather ship, learn, and iterate than perfect a spec.

    Build with what you own and form opinions through first-hand use, from creating a project to configuring the policies around it.

    Use AI tools to compress research, drafting, and feedback synthesis so you can focus on judgment calls.

    Work async by default, making decisions in writing in a fully remote team.

    Recent findings suggest that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Sources indicate that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    Industry observers note that once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    It has been revealed that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    The New York Times is adding more AI features to its Cooking app, and users aren’t thrilled

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • In a recent development, sometimes, adding just one new ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.11Olives, yecch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    In a recent development, sometimes, adding just one new ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.11Olives, yecch. And that’s how at least some New York Times readers see its addition of AI features to its popular Cooking app.

    Here’s Genevieve Ko, NYT Cooking senior editor and columnist, explaining the new features:.

    I naïvely assumed A.I. wouldn’t affect my work as a recipe developer and my role at NYT Cooking, where I oversee the editorial side of our recipes and related stories. But as artificial intelligence improved, our product and engineering colleagues saw its potential to help us create features Cooking users wanted.

    The Times had previously rolled out AI features aimed at converting volume-based and weight-based measurements (“What’s one cup of bok choy in grams?”) and scaling a recipe up or down to serve more or fewer people. The main fresh feature is focused on ingredient substitutions.

    Recent findings suggest that say you’re cooking braised white beans and greens with parmesan, NYT Cooking app in hand. But you notice that you’re out of chard and only have spinach. Cooking veterans know that chard is a rough-and-tumble green that has some backbone22There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.”, while spinach is a comparative wimp that will wilt the moment you look at it funny. If you need to sub in spinach for chard, how would the recipe change? Would you, for instance, add the spinach later than you would the chard to account for its pathetic stamina? That’s the sort of thing the new AI feature could account for.

    Cooking staffers “spent countless hours evaluating sample after sample to get the chatbot answers to closely align with how we would answer as culinary experts,” Ko writes. “We applied the same rigor as we do to editing, grounded in Times standards.”.

    According to recent reports, but because Ko knows that any AI-powered features are likely to be controversial with a Times audience, she spends quite a lot of space addressing potential objections, everything from “the impact of data centers” to “the concentration of power among A.I. companies” and “the risk of A.I. escaping our control.” These features are designed to enable “the tactile physical pleasure of cooking” and getting a “very real, very human creation” on your table.

    Broadly speaking, commenters weren’t buying it.

    “What a massive disappointment,” wrote Susan from Fresh Jersey. “The internet is full of AI cooking content. I pay you because I prefer mine done by people.”.

    According to recent reports, “This decision misses the mark by such a wide margin it’s baffling,” says Ian from Los Angeles. “And the disclosure just as baffling. It would not be inaccurate to summarize the piece as saying ‘I know doing this is bad and I don’t want to be associated with the bad thing so that’s why we are doing the bad thing.'”.

    According to recent reports, “Nobody wants this, it’s bad for cooking, it’s bad for the NYT,” writes Bill from Pittsburgh. “Wasting a column trying to gaslight yourself and your audience into believing that it’s anything but is an embarrassment and a waste of everyone’s time.”.

    “PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE DO NOT DO THIS,” says Judah Mann of Fresh York. “Oh, wait, you already did. Ok, I’m out.”.

    Or as Naomi from California puts it: “I am sad that AI has breached the one online resource I truly love.”.

    Because I enjoy the irony, I scraped the 171 comments left on the Times’ announcement and asked Codex (running GPT-6.1 Sol, at medium thinking) to do some sentiment analysis. (Twelve of the 171 were comments left by Times staffers; I’m excluding them here.) Roughly 77% of the reader comments were negative about the newly introduced AI features, it found, versus 14% positive and the remainder neutral or mixed. Among the biggest categories of complaint: This shouldn’t require AI. AI is destroying the environment. AI is not why I’m paying the Times $390 a year. The adjustments the AI produces are going to be bad.

    In a recent development, dozens of commenters asked for a way to turn off the feature. “No, not at this time,” Ko responded, “though this feature is completely optional to use.” Indeed: Don’t ask AI to substitute your chard and AI won’t substitute your chard.

    One consistent thread was that cooking is supposed to present you with difficulties and challenges and the whole point is figuring them out by yourself. “Anyone using AI for cooking has no sense of taste and no desire to work out the intricacies of cooking and baking,” writes Michael King from Brooklyn. “To use AI for recipes is beyond the pale. If you are going to use AI, then just cut to the chase and defenestrate yourself.” Or BJ from North Carolina: “So, you’re telling me that I’m too stupid to figure it out on my own?”.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, the few positive comments tended to focus on how the AI feature had, in fact, made dietary substitutions easier for them. “I love the latest AI feature because it rapidly (and so far) accurately converts recipes to gluten free,” Anne Wagner from Kansas City writes. “I don’t cook for stress relief,” indicates Andy from San Francisco. “I cook to put dinner on the table. Anything that makes the process a little faster or smoother is welcome.”.

    Microsoft Rebuilds Its Smart Bidding Prediction Models, Rolling Out Automatically via @sejournal, @brookeosmundson

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Microsoft Advertising is rolling out what it calls its biggest bidding model upgrade in a decade.
    • Microsoft will apply the upgrade automatically as it reaches more accounts.
    • According to recent reports, microsoft states the latest models can change how rapidly campaigns spend and how closely they stick to your targets.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Microsoft Advertising is rolling out what it calls its biggest bidding model upgrade in a decade. The newly introduced models use more signals to predict whether an ad click will turn into a conversion and what it might be worth.

    Microsoft will apply the upgrade automatically as it reaches more accounts. That means campaigns can start spending differently before you make any changes yourself. Microsoft confirmed the rollout on November 18 and aims more bidding updates in 2027.

    According to recent reports, microsoft states the latest models can change how rapidly campaigns spend and how closely they stick to your targets. These are the areas to keep an eye on:.

    A $50 CPA target still leaves room for a campaign to bring in conversions at $40 each, even if it spends its full budget. A max CPC can limit that flexibility. Say you average $3 a click and cap bids at $5. The cap rules out a $6 bid even if Microsoft expects the click could bring in a conversion within your CPA target.

    Say you raise your CPA target on Monday and customers usually take a week to buy. By Friday, you know what Monday’s clicks cost, but you may still be waiting on some of the sales. Faster bidding won’t shorten the time those customers take to buy.

    Sources indicate that raising a CPA target or lowering a ROAS target can open up auctions your campaign previously passed up. To limit swings in performance, Microsoft suggests making those changes in 15% increments and reviewing each after one conversion cycle. For a bigger change, like switching bid strategies or adding a conversion goal, Microsoft recommends allowing one to two cycles.

    In a recent development, microsoft recommends conversion-based bidding for newly introduced campaigns once the account has at least five conversions. Those can come from campaigns you already run. If you’re still gathering your first five, Enhanced CPC is an option.

    On LinkedIn, Sophie Westall asked if the same advice applies to low-volume accounts already using Enhanced CPC. Microsoft Advertising Liaison Navah Hopkins replied:.

    Every account is different so a blanket recommendation still needs to be put to the test. With that noted, so long as the account has at least 5 conversions total, the system is smart enough to use that to begin with conversion-based bidding. While we still recommend the 30-day evaluation period and not making too many changes if you’re working with fewer conversions, the system is much more responsive now!

    For judging performance, Microsoft recommends around 30 conversions in 30 days at the campaign or portfolio level. A low-volume campaign can reach the end of that first month and still have too few conversions to judge the switch.

    Recent findings suggest that microsoft reported 10% more conversion value per click at roughly the same ROAS after the model upgrade. That result came from August 2026 global Search and Audience Network data for advertisers using Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS.

    Microsoft also looked at advertisers who switched bid strategies. Search advertisers who moved from Target CPA to Target ROAS saw 8% more conversion value at a similar ROAS. Advertisers who moved from Enhanced CPC to Maximize Conversions with a CPA target saw 18% more conversions at a similar CPA.

    It has been revealed that if you’re considering Target ROAS, pull up a few recent purchases in Microsoft Advertising and compare the reported values with the order totals. A $40 order and a $400 order can both show up as conversions even if your tracking assigns them the same value. That’s easy to miss if you’re used to checking that purchases are coming through and leaving it there.

    Microsoft reported its largest gains from value-based bidding among advertisers who sent actual transaction values. If your purchase goal uses a fixed value, the reported ROAS reflects that estimate. It can move as you sell more or spend less, but it won’t capture a change in how much customers spend per order.

    It has been revealed that with lead gen, you may need time to get a better read on what a conversion is worth. Two people can submit the same form, and sales may find out a week later that only one is a fit.

    Pedro Bailaderia asked Navah Hopkins about sending an estimate at submission and updating it once more information comes into the CRM. Hopkins supported using the Conversions API or offline imports. She also advised setting a ROAS target that reflects the values you send.

    If your team is still working out how to value a qualified lead, that’s worth settling before you set a ROAS target. A campaign can hit the target you set while sales is still waiting for more leads it can work with.

    If a campaign already brings in the sales or leads you need at a cost you’re happy with, you can give the upgrade some room before changing anything. Keeping your settings steady makes it easier to see how the fresh models work with the goals and budget you already have.

    Recent findings suggest that the rollout may be more useful if you’ve been adjusting targets to get a campaign to spend more evenly. If delivery settles down on its own, you may have fewer reasons to touch those targets during the week. That would leave you freer to change them when the business needs more volume or can afford to pay more for a conversion.

    About six in 10 Americans mentioned they have at least “some” confidence that news organizations will report the upcoming midterm election results accurately, according to a new national survey. But only 32% said they had “quite a bit” or “a great deal” of confidence that journalists would do the job.

    In the survey from Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media, 37% noted they had either “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” that news outlets would accurately report the election results.

    The survey was completed by a nationally representative sample of 1,057 U.S. adults either online or by telephone earlier this month. The findings echo other national surveys, including a Gallup survey that revealed trust in media to report “fully, accurately, and fairly” at 33% — an increase from an all-time low last year.

    The Medill/Alliance survey found about half of Americans said they had “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” in news outlets to investigate voter fraud claims thoroughly. U.S. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on elections on 70% of days since returning to office — starting with false claims about voter fraud on the first day of his second term.

    In another bleak result from the same poll, slightly more survey respondents remarked journalists manipulate the news for political or commercial purposes than report it accurately. Across the survey, Democrats reported being more confident in (and trusting of) news organizations than Republicans. Nearly 80% of Republicans said journalists try to manipulate the news compared to 38% of independents and 24% of Democrats.

    More on the survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, here.

    #66902. Breaking: Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4336 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4336 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try newly introduced things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try newly introduced things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

    Most local newsrooms in the U.S. have one thing in common: They need more money, and many dream of dollars they can use however they want.

    RELATED ARTICLEPress Forward awards $20 million to 205 small local newsroomsSophie CulpepperOctober 16, 2024In 2024, Press Forward, the nonprofit trying to mobilize a philanthropic army for local news, announced it would give at least 100 small local newsrooms — those with annual budgets under $1 million — just that type of unrestricted funding. Almost 1,000 newsrooms applied. Ultimately, Press Forward distributed $20 million to 205 outlets. Most of them received $100,000 each, split over two years.

    I wondered what the recipients had done with the money, and which problems it had (or hadn’t) solved. Between May and October, I spoke or emailed with more than 30 grantees.

    The grantees represented every U.S. state, came from cities, suburbs, and rural areas, and published in multiple languages. They included for-profits and nonprofits, print and digital-only publications, college newsrooms, and public radio stations. Statewide newsrooms with fully staffed teams like The Maine Monitor, scrappy news startups like 285 South, and community newspapers powered by freelancers and part-time staff like the Copper River Record in Alaska all received funding.

    For many newsrooms, Press Forward was the first grant they’d ever applied for. “Many of the country’s newsrooms are small, and few get foundation grants,” stated Press Forward executive director Dale Anglin. The open call was designed to change that and to distribute the money quickly. Grantees were required to complete two LION sustainability audits a year apart; Press Forward is analyzing that data now and will release its findings next month.1.

    Recent findings suggest that RELATED ARTICLEA study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundationSeth C. LewisOctober 6, 2026“People tell me that what Press Forward did was unusual and rare within philanthropy,” stated María José Ramírez Braiz, founder and CEO of Midwest-based grantee Te Lo Cuento News.

    In a recent development, “They mentioned to us at the beginning of the grant period, before the shit hit the fan with the federal government, ‘If you need this money to keep the lights on, keep the lights on,'” said Copper River Record editor Allison Sayer, one of the paper’s two part-time staffers. “I feel that this was really a gift.”.

    Industry observers note that first-time grant applicants and recipients, in particular, stated Press Forward’s recognition gave them credibility and visibility with other funders. And publishers described the funding as a morale boost that validated low-paid work.

    In a recent development, “It has been a life-changer, a lifesaver for us,” noted Gretchen Sporleder Orr, who publishes the World Journal in southern Colorado with her husband. Her voice broke when she talked to me about the funding. “I don’t know if we would be in business right now if it wasn’t for the Press Forward money.”.

    Industry observers note that the Real WV “would not still exist without Press Forward,” remarked Stephen Baldwin, the site’s volunteer publisher. (He’s also the former minority leader for the West Virginia Senate and a pastor of two churches.) The outlet was one of eight grantees that received just two $25,000 grants over two years. “There’s not exactly a lot of capital floating around West Virginia for nonprofit news,” Baldwin said, “and without this outside impact, we wouldn’t be able to do this work.” But he hopes that the site can be less reliant on grants in the future.

    The funding did not save every recipient. One grantee, Atlanta Civic Circle, shut down earlier this year. Atlanta Civic Circle did not receive its second $50,000 grant because it didn’t complete the first LION audit, Anglin remarked. (Atlanta Civic Circle did not respond to my request for an interview, but executive director Saba Long wrote on LinkedIn in June that “the funding environment for local nonprofit journalism is extraordinarily difficult right now.”) Other recipients have merged or transformed since applying for the grant.2.

    It has been revealed that RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026Medill’s annual State of Local News report, released this month, describes a local news ecosystem in a “state of precarity.” That state of precariousness helps explain how $100,000 over two years can be a “godsend,” a “miracle,” and not enough. As one grantee put it, “Right now, these are shanties built on a beach, waiting for a hurricane to come through.”.

    “Press Forward reached newsrooms that don’t have existing relationships with major national funders,” noted Nina Ignaczak, the founder, publisher, and editor of Planet Detroit. “The challenge now is whether the commitment holds.”.

    The funding helped newsrooms keep the lights on, whether they used it to pay bills, pay down debt, make payroll, or as a buffer when something went wrong.

    “The flexibility that Press Forward has given us has allowed us to fill — I wouldn’t say emergencies, but unexpected gaps,” noted Richard Young, founder and executive director of CivicLex in Kentucky. It brought on a consulting editor to keep city hall coverage going after losing a reporter, and purchased newly introduced software. Without the funding, CivicLex likely would have had to dip into its reserves, he said.

    Bob Bonnar, publisher of the News Letter Journal in Wyoming, used the first payment from Press Forward to upgrade computers and cameras and give some staffers raises. “That chewed up the money very swiftly,” he said, “and I probably should have held some of it back because the News Letter Journal ended up having a pretty rough year in 2025.” He had to use about half of the second $50,000 payment to repay an operating loan. The rest covered the remaining revenue shortfall and kept the organization in the black through the winter.

    Vandana Kumar, publisher of the California-based ethnic media outlet India Currents, described the funding as a “stabilizing force” that allowed the newsroom to keep operating despite a contraction in philanthropic giving and cuts to local government advertising.

    The Copper River Record built infrastructure to host digital ads and created a newly introduced website. It held listening sessions with Native villages in its coverage area and donated subscriptions to local Tribal offices. It improved the design of its print newspaper. Sayer paid freelancers to complete Press Pass training and pursued other professional development. And she was able to take on more ambitious stories about PFAS and “forever chemicals.”.

    The Press Forward funding was “the biggest single windfall in nearly 20 years for our small community newspaper,” Sandpoint Reader publisher Ben Olson told me. The Idaho-based paper used the money to travel to the state capital for Press Club awards and design a newly introduced media kit, which Olson said has improved ad sales. The Reader also paid a large chunk of its printing bill, paid its rent a year in advance, and gave staffers bonuses. (The bonuses helped the paper become 100% employee-owned; Olson’s two employees bought in when Olson’s business partner and co-owner retired.).

    Sources indicate that the open-ended nature of the grants gave Colorado’s World Journal “the flexibility to be able to make a change, do a thing, and then pivot as needed,” Sporleder Orr said. “When we were in the toilet, all I could think about was, like, ‘Is there going to be anything in the post office today so that I can make payroll?’ ‘Oh, my God, we’ve got to pay rent.’” Sometimes she and her husband skipped their own paychecks to pay staff. The grant gave them “emotional bandwidth” to blueprint ahead.

    Recent findings suggest that many grantees used the funding to hire full- or part-time staffers. Sometimes, that worked out well.

    According to recent reports, the Mānoa Mirror, an online newsroom based at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, received two $25,000 grants, which it used to hire a managing editor, a student editorial coordinator, three student reporters, and a social media producer. (The managing editor was paid a stipend, and the other positions were part-time.) The work had previously depended on “faculty goodwill and volunteerism, which was not sustainable for long,” said Hye-ryeon Lee, who was professor and chair of the school of communication and information until retiring this summer. With the new hires, the site went from publishing a few stories a month to publishing daily.

    The Real WV’s first LION audit pointed to a need its small team had already recognized: hiring someone to sell ads. It hired a public school teacher with sales experience (including selling ads for the yearbook) part-time.

    It has been revealed that the funding allowed Te Lo Cuento News to pay contributors consistently and to add contract, part-time positions including a sales manager, an office administrator, and a couple of reporters. The only position it could sustain beyond the grant period is the part-time sales manager, Ramírez Braiz said.

    Sources indicate that the Texas Spur is one of five weekly newspapers owned by Paragraph Ranch Media. Originally, the team planned to use the Press Forward grant to secure a loan to improve organization housing and hire a journalist based in Spur (population 863 as of 2020). But nobody took the newspaper up on the free housing offer, said editor and general manager Barbara Brannon. So the company hired four early-career journalists (two full-time, two part-time) living in its 10-county coverage area. Three of the four left for jobs in other industries halfway through their second year. The one who stayed is doing well as a regional sports reporter, Brannon said, and a hire who replaced a person who left is now managing editor for The Post Dispatch.3.

    Industry observers note that the turnover Brannon experienced isn’t unique to Spur. Other newsrooms also found hiring with grant money challenging.

    Sometimes, that was because of location. “Had we been able to find the right people from the outset, I believe the grant would have had a greater impact on the business,” said Anton Kaufer, regional publisher for Hagadone Media Montana. In rural Northwest Montana, though, recruiting and retaining staff is a challenge, and Hagadone’s Mineral Independent struggled to replace its salesperson and office manager after they retired. The experience “reinforced for us that sustainability isn’t just about having the funding,” Kaufer said. “It’s also about having the people in place to make the most of it.”.

    According to recent reports, the World Journal tried placing an ad for a salesperson with the Colorado Press Association and got “absolutely no interest,” Sporleder Orr said. “People living in northern Colorado don’t particularly want to come live in a teeny-tiny town in a rural, broke part of the state.” (She credited the grant with giving her the mental space to fire a salesperson who wasn’t working out, then regroup.).

    Sources indicate that other times, the money just wasn’t enough. “The reality is that $100,000 over two years isn’t a lot,” one grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. “You can’t hire somebody with that.”.

    EcoRI’s experience illustrates those limitations. Before receiving the Press Forward grant, EcoRI had used other grant funding and reserves to hire a director of development in a one-year contract position. In its grant application to Press Forward, the team proposed converting that role into a full-time staff position with benefits.

    According to recent reports, the salary limited the hiring pool, though. The development director position paid $65,000 a year, which “is really not the market rate for a director of development” in the area, publisher and cofounder Jo Detz stated. (She said it should be more like $90,000.) The staffer they ended up hiring came from another state and hadn’t worked in news before. In a staff position, he cost more than he was bringing in. Detz laid him off and eliminated the position last December. She called the experience “heartbreaking.”.

    “At the point where I knew this wasn’t working,” she noted, “there wasn’t enough runway to pivot, rethink, rehire.”.

    Recent findings suggest that beyond the salary limitations, Detz thinks the development director didn’t have enough runway to succeed. The kind of development the staffer was hired to oversee — major gifts and individual giving — is a long game; “that position would need at least two or three years to begin to see some benefits,” she said. Now, she’s back where she started, juggling fundraising with her other work.

    “I know it’s crazy to say that $100,000 over two years wasn’t enough,” she remarked, “but it was not enough to make a meaningful difference to our revenue strategy.”.

    Planet Detroit’s Ignaczak was in a unique position: Around the same time the newsroom received the Press Forward grant, Planet Detroit also received a $500,000 three-year grant from the MacArthur Foundation. That grant allowed her to hire a managing editor, she said.

    Ignaczak believes general operating support is what small nonprofit newsrooms need. But to be effective, “I really think fully funding a revenue role for a minimum of three years is what needs to happen to build sustainability, if that is the goal,” she mentioned. “And $100,000 over two years is not enough to achieve that.”.

    NotiVisión Georgia, a Spanish-language local news outlet with one full-time staffer, is committed to print in a world moving away from it. The print newspaper is the only way the outlet has been able to use to “generate real economic value,” said CEO Mónica Pirela, because it’s where local companies want to place ads. The organization spent some of its Press Forward funds on printing and distribution. Pirela wears “every hat” right now, and the organization’s top need is a dedicated sales manager, she said.

    California’s BenitoLink, meanwhile, used some of the Press Forward funding to begin printing in 2025. That will allow it to apply for newspaper of record status and get paid for running legal notices.

    Industry observers note that in Minnesota, Swift County Monitor-News publisher and owner Reed Anfinson called the grant a “godsend” at a time when tariffs and rising gas prices have driven up printing and delivery costs and weakened advertisers’ budgets. The for-profit Monitor-News put some of its Press Forward funding toward redesigning its print newspaper. Anfinson also purchased materials as part of an “Out of Sight/Out of Mind” advertising campaign stressing the value of print. (He created the campaign himself, using Midjourney for the images.) For news organizations in small towns, Anfinson believes, digital revenue will never be enough to sustain operations.

    Some organizations used the funding to expand their remit beyond news.

    For instance, the Copper River Record partnered with the Copper River Native Association to include weekly language graphics in the paper for Ahtna, a critically endangered language, coordinating with a local kindergarten class. That project required a lot of time and investment up front, Sayer mentioned, but it can continue beyond the life of the grant.

    In a recent development, planet Detroit used some Press Forward funding for reporting, but “the most significant thing the grant made possible wasn’t any single story,” Ignaczak noted. The grant gave the team time to work on its Civic Action Toolbox, which turns reporting into civic engagement prompts. In a story about a local ballot proposal, for instance, the embedded toolbox flags upcoming public meetings, links to contact information for local representatives, and suggests an organization to follow. The tool is also in beta testing with other newsrooms.

    “The whole project came from having the space to ask what our readers actually need from us beyond information, and then building toward that,” Ignaczak mentioned. “Unrestricted funding makes that kind of work possible.”.

    Anfinson of the Monitor-News took the unusual step of writing a grant application on behalf of the local school district, which was losing students to adjacent districts. He used some of the Press Forward funding to match a $2,500 grant to the district. The district then ran $5,000 in ads in a “goodwill effort” to stem declining enrollment. The partnership helped to raise the Monitor-News’s profile, he said, by highlighting the benefits of newspaper advertising.

    Recent findings suggest that press Forward required grantees to complete two LION sustainability audits. But it also offered optional coaching via the media consulting company Blue Engine to help implement the first audit’s recommendations. Of the 205 grantees, 154 participated in coaching, Anglin said.

    The coaching kicked off in January, with most individual coaches and grantees meeting monthly. Multiple participants remarked the support would have been more beneficial if it were introduced earlier. This was a tradeoff of Press Forward moving promptly to get money out the door, Anglin said.4.

    This was the first large, unrestricted grant Austin Common had ever received, and it struggled with how to spend the money. “It felt like a lot of pressure,” noted Amy Stansbury, the site’s editor-in-chief and only full-time staffer.

    Stansbury wanted to bring on the organization’s first full-time employees, but didn’t want to make those hires (and spend all the grant money) until she had a clear plan. The coaching helped her figure out which hires made the most strategic sense and how to budget for them.

    A few publishers were lukewarm about the substance of the coaching, but the majority I heard from were enthusiastic. At first, Baldwin was skeptical and worried the coaching might amount to “checking a box.” In practice, though, he remarked it’s been “tremendously helpful” for tasks like writing the job description for the Real WV’s sales position.

    Sources indicate that sporleder Orr called the coaching “incredible.” The monthly sessions helped her with everything from tackling grant proposals to improving her Google Analytics skills. The combination of money and coaching, she added, “makes sure that the recipients don’t just continue doing business as usual.”.

    In addition to the funding, Press Forward paid for grantees to attend conferences. Anglin remarked 111 grantees attended the Lenfest News Philanthropy Summit in Philadelphia in 2025, 81 attended the same conference (which I also attended) in 2026, and 87 attended the Business of Local conference in Salt Lake City in 2025. A handful of grantees attended affinity conferences.

    Stansbury found attending conferences for the first time helpful and eye-opening. It taught her “there’s this secret shadow world of [invitation-only] foundation and grant funding.” Press Forward’s travel support to attend a national conference was “transformative” for India Currents, Kumar stated, giving it visibility and access to relationship-building.

    In a recent development, to small newsrooms, the grant felt like a Press Forward stamp of approval that put them on the map for other funders. The Mirror’s Lee called the Press Forward funding “instrumental” in securing a $20,000 grant from a local foundation. But that was an exception among publishers I heard from; most didn’t feel the visibility and credibility conferred by the grant directly translated to other funders giving them more money.

    So several publishers, including Ramírez Braiz of Te Lo Cuento News, would like to see Press Forward go a step further and make individual introductions to funders. “Those more personal introductions can make a major difference for small organizations,” she said.

    Ramírez Braiz also called for “more shared learning around outcomes and impact.” Few grantees had a good sense of what others in the cohort were up to, and some were interested in more knowledge sharing with peer organizations, though the day-to-day grind of keeping one’s own newsroom running was a common impediment.

    Since 2023, Anglin mentioned, Press Forward’s network of more than 130 funders has invested $258 million directly in newsrooms. That suggests that over half of the more than $400 million the coalition says it’s invested has gone to newsrooms.

    According to recent reports, when Press Forward first declared the direct funding for newsrooms, it “felt really awesome,” the grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. To the grantee, it was meaningful to see Press Forward give funding to more organizations than planned in response to the scale of need. But when Press Forward went on to a second funding round in which single organizations, including both newsrooms and newsroom-adjacent organizations like the International Women’s Media Foundation and LION, received as much as $1.5 million for infrastructure projects, the same grantee remarked it felt like “a slap in the face.”.

    “Many of the problems newsrooms face aren’t unique to them individually,” Anglin mentioned. “If we are attempting to solve problems at scale, we have to intervene not just at the newsroom level, but at the systems level, too.” She said that because many of the infrastructure grantees serve multiple newsrooms, “investing in them creates a multiplier effect across the industry.”.

    Sources indicate that the argument that funding support organizations and infrastructure lifts more boats is “a cop-out,” this publisher noted. “I think the philanthropists know it, I think the associations know it, and I think the potential grantees that are not funders or associations or intermediaries know it.”.

    Sources indicate that young had a different perspective. Because of CivicLex’s broad scope, it seeks out funding from both democracy funders and journalism funders. Young thinks local news funders are way ahead on getting dollars into local communities.

    According to recent reports, “I think Press Forward has done one of the more effective jobs of anything I’ve seen in the broader landscape of my world, and the civic renewal space, of delivering resources to the local level,” he said. (He added, “No one is ever happy in the local news ecosystem when I say that folks in the local news ecosystem don’t know how good they have it. That does not win me a lot of friends.”).

    Most publishers I heard from see grants like this as critical to continued operation, yet they’re wary of overreliance on philanthropy.

    In a recent development, young mentioned he’d be surprised if local news is still a focus for national philanthropy in eight years. “Filling your cup up with money that will be impossible to recover in four years is a danger zone,” he added.

    Right now, more than 80% of Planet Detroit’s revenue mix comes from foundations. Ignaczak mentioned the organization hopes to bring that down to 50% by 2028. “But for nonprofit newsrooms covering environmental and public health issues in a mid-size metro, general operating grants aren’t a crutch,” she said. “They’re infrastructure.”.

    In a recent development, as for Press Forward, “Time will tell, as these grants go away, what impact [they’ve] actually had on the newsrooms that received [them], how many have managed to build sustainability,” she added. “I think a newsroom that needed $50,000 to survive to next year had problems that $50,000 isn’t going to solve.”.

    Sources indicate that LOOKOUT executive director Jake Hylton believes there’s enough funding to go around. “While there may not be enough to support every single newsroom at a very large amount,” he mentioned, “I do believe that there is a larger investment in news that could be done.”.

    In a recent development, A second grantee who asked to stay anonymous was blunt about their fears for the future. “We’re scared shitless about 2027,” this person stated, “because not only is the Press Forward money not returning, we also see none of the national grants that sustained us in 2024 and previous years.”.

    The Copper River Record was in the black before receiving this grant, and the lean paper’s fixed overhead remains low. For the Record, Press Forward has been like “a fairy godmother,” Sayer mentioned.

    “I’m not going to lie: I will miss having the money to say yes to any reasonable story,” she continued. “But I think that, even going back to our original budget, the strength of what we learned will continue to help us deliver a higher quality paper that is more relevant to the communities we serve.”.

    The Sandpoint Reader, Olson said, is “surviving” right now. “We’d love to be thriving,” he added, “but we’re happy to continue to survive when many print publications aren’t.” He credited the Press Forward grant with giving the burned-out team “the chance to fall in love with our industry again.”.

    Sporleder Orr feels nervous about what’s ahead, but with the World Journal in a much more comfortable cash flow position, she and her husband are “in a way better mental state about the business.”.

    Sources indicate that “We feel good about the future right now, that we are going to be able to keep going and make it,” she remarked. “We’re back to, ‘This is what we do ’til we die.'”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that cloudLinux is the maker of Imunify360 — a suite of security products protecting millions of websites across the web hosting industry — and of CloudLinux OS, the operating system behind a large share of the world's shared hosting. To learn more about our company and products, visit our websites: cloudlinux.com and imunify360.com. Alongside those established product lines we run a small innovation team whose job is to find and prove the next ones.

    We are looking for a Product Owner to lead that team: a small, senior, fully remote squad of engineers that takes new product concepts from idea to a working MVP in customers' hands, then hands proven products to a product line and moves on to the next concept. You will be accountable for the pipeline of ideas, the speed and rigour with which they are tested, and the evidence behind every go / no-go recommendation.

    This is a hands-on lead role, not pure people management: roughly 50% discovery and leadership (customer conversations, scoping, prioritisation, coaching, reporting to the CPO) and 50% building (prototypes, spikes, design and code review, demo stands). You will not be the team's only builder, but you must be able to build a credible prototype yourself and hold a technical opinion about every part of it.

    You don't need to arrive as an expert in web hosting or security. If you have taken a product from nothing to its first paying customers before — as a founder, an early engineer, or the lead of an incubation team — and you get deep into unfamiliar technical territory fast, we will teach you the market.

    The innovation team sits across CloudLinux and Imunify and owns the product concepts that do not yet have a home in an established product line. Ideas come from customer conversations, industry events, telemetry across more than 80,000 servers and the CPO’s strategy; the team’s job is to turn them into something a customer will pay for within a quarter, using AI coding agents throughout.

    Prototyping and technical direction.

    According to recent reports, we evaluate engineers partly on how effectively they work with coding agents, and in the innovation team this is the main lever on speed. As the lead you model and coach it: prompt specificity, review quality on agent-generated code, context provision, iteration and error recovery, and end-to-end task completion. Expect to use agents to build prototypes, generate test corpora and draft customer-facing material.
